sources.text:
DECISION TREE · MECHANICS
How a Decision Tree Splits Data
1 Start with all training examples sitting at the root node.
2 For every candidate feature, measure how ‘impure’ (mixed) the resulting groups would 
be.
3 Pick the split that gains the most information — i.e. cuts impurity the most.
4 Repeat this process inside each child node, recursively.
5 Stop at a max depth / min sample count, or when a node is pure — that node becomes 
a leaf that predicts the majority class.
Entropy(S) = −Σ pᵢ log₂(pᵢ)      Information Gain = Entropy(parent) − 
Σ (|child|/|parent|)·Entropy(child)

sources.topic: Decision Tree Splitting Criterion (Entropy & Information Gain)
sources.text:
DECISION TREE · WORKED EXAMPLE
Choosing the Root Split — Loan Default Data
# Income Credit History Default?
1 High Good No
2 High Good No
3 High Bad Yes
4 Low Good No
5 Low Good Yes
6 Low Bad Yes
7 Low Bad Yes
8 High Bad Yes
Step 1 — Overall entropy (5 Yes / 3 No)
Entropy(S) = −(5/8)log₂(5/8) − (3/8)log₂(3/8) = 0.424 + 0.531 = 0.954
Step 2 — Split on Credit History (Good / Bad)
Good (4): 1 Yes / 3 No → entropy = 0.811      Bad (4): 4 Yes / 0 No → entropy = 0
Weighted entropy = (4/8)(0.811) + (4/8)(0) = 0.406      →  IG = 0.954 − 0.406 = 0.549
Step 3 — Split on Income (High / Low)
High (4): 2 Yes / 2 No → entropy = 1.000      Low (4): 3 Yes / 1 No → entropy = 0.811
Weighted entropy = (4/8)(1.000) + (4/8)(0.811) = 0.906      →  IG = 0.954 − 0.906 = 0.049

sources.text:
ROADMAP
What We’ll Cover
1
Decision Tree
A single tree that splits data by asking the question that separates classes best.
2
Random Forest
Hundreds of independent trees, each trained on a random slice of the data, voting together.
3
K-Means Clustering
No labels needed — the algorithm groups similar points together by repeatedly moving toward the nearest centroid.
Each section covers: how the model works → a worked example with real numbers → applications, merits & demerits.

sources.topic: Decision Tree Splitting Criterion (Entropy & Information Gain)
sources.text:
DECISION TREE · IN PRACTICE
Where It's Used — and Its Trade-offs
APPLICATIONS
Credit scoring rules · Medical triage / diagnosis checklists · Customer-churn flagging · Simple fraud-alert rules · Any setting where a human must read and 
approve the model's logic
MERITS
✓ Fully interpretable — you can read the exact decision path (a “white box” 
model)
✓ No feature scaling or normalisation needed
✓ Naturally handles both numeric and categorical features
✓ Cheap and fast to train and to score new records
DEMERITS
✗ Prone to overfitting — a fully grown tree can memorise noise
✗ Unstable: a small change in data can produce a very different tree
✗ Biased toward features with many distinct values/levels
✗ Poor at extrapolating beyond the range seen in training (regression)
SUPERVISED LEARNING 05 / 13

sources.topic: Decision Tree Splitting Criterion (Entropy & Information Gain)
sources.text:
RANDOM FOREST · IN PRACTICE
Where It's Used — and Its Trade-offs
APPLICATIONS
Fraud & anomaly detection · Satellite / land-cover classification · Feature-importance ranking in genomics · Recommendation pre-filtering · Any tabular 
problem needing solid accuracy without heavy tuning
MERITS
✓ Much lower variance than a single tree — far less prone to overfitting
✓ Handles high-dimensional, messy, or partially missing data well
✓ Gives a built-in feature-importance ranking for free
✓ Trees train independently — easy to parallelise across cores
DEMERITS
✗ Loses the single-tree's easy interpretability — harder to explain a 
prediction
✗ Slower to train and to score than one tree (hundreds of trees)
✗ Larger memory footprint to store the whole ensemble
✗ Can still overfit if trees are grown too deep on noisy labels
SUPERVISED LEARNING 08 / 13

sources.topic: Decision Tree Splitting Criterion (Entropy & Information Gain)
sources.text:
SIDE BY SIDE
How the Three Models Compare
Aspect Decision Tree Random Forest K-Means Clustering
Learning type Supervised Supervised Unsupervised
Core mechanism Splits on the feature that gains the most 
information Bags many trees and lets them vote / average Assigns points to the nearest of k centroids
Primarily optimizes Information gain per split Variance (via averaging) Within-cluster sum of squares
Interpretability High — readable rules Medium — needs importance plots Medium — visualize clusters, inspect centroids
Training speed Fast Moderate, parallelisable Fast, but repeats over all points each iteration
Key risk High if unpruned Lower, self-averaging Sensitive to k and to starting centroids
Rule of thumb: start with a single tree to understand the data, move to a Random Forest for a robust supervised baseline, and reach for K-Means when you have no labels and want 
to discover structure in the data itself.
SUPERVISED & UNSUPERVISED LEARNING 12 / 13

sources.topic: Decision Tree Splitting Criterion (Entropy & Information Gain)
sources.text:
KEY TAKEAWAYS
It's a Trade-off, Not a Ranking
1 Decision Tree
The building block. Fast and fully interpretable, but a single tree is unstable and overfits easily on its own.
2 Random Forest
Trades a little interpretability for stability — bagging many independent trees averages away their individual noise.
3 K-Means Clustering
A different kind of tool entirely — no labels needed, just groups points by proximity to find structure you didn't know to look for.
Choose based on what the problem needs most: a readable rule, a stable baseline, or hidden structure in unlabeled data.
